title: Cinderella and the Lantern-Lit Ball

story_parts.intro: Once upon a time, in a quiet corner of a castle town surrounded by green hills, there lived a gentle girl named Cinderella. Her home was a cozy wooden house with a tatami kitchen and a warm irori hearth in the middle of the floor. Outside, a little garden held a stone lantern and a pond where golden koi swam round and round. But Cinderella was not happy there. After her father passed away, her Stepmother and her two Stepsisters came to live in the house, and they made Cinderella do all the work. From morning until night, she swept the tatami mats, cooked the rice, and tended the irori fire while her ash and soot-covered kimono grew gray with dust. "Hurry up, Cinderella!" the Stepmother would say in a sharp voice. "The floor must shine before supper!" The Stepsisters giggled behind their sleeves. "Look at her! She looks like a little chimney!" they teased. But Cinderella only smiled softly and kept working, because her heart was full of kindness, even on the hardest days. One crisp autumn day, a messenger arrived from the palace with wonderful news. The Prince was holding a grand banquet at the castle, and every young lady in town was invited! The Stepmother and Stepsisters squealed with delight and began preparing their most elaborate formal kimono, with ornate hairpins and silk obi sashes. "May I come too?" Cinderella asked hopefully. The Stepmother laughed coldly. "You? At the palace? Who would cook and clean while we are away? Absolutely not!" Then the family swept out the door in their finery, leaving Cinderella all alone by the irori hearth, with tears rolling quietly down her cheeks.
story_parts.developpement: Just then, a warm light filled the kitchen, and a kind old woman appeared, her wand twinkling with tiny stars. "Do not cry, dear child," said the Fairy Godmother gently. "You shall go to the ball after all!" With a swirl of her sparkling wand, Cinderella's ragged clothes became a shimmering kimono-style gown, glowing like moonlight on water, with a beautiful obi sash and delicate glass slippers on her feet. "Kirei! How beautiful!" Cinderella whispered, twirling around. Next, the Fairy Godmother waved her wand at a humble palanquin resting in the garden, and it became a magnificent ornate kago, grand enough for a princess. Six white mice grew into snowy horses to carry it, and a sleepy old dog became a fine coachman. "Now listen carefully," said the Fairy Godmother, her eyes kind but serious. "When the temple bell rings midnight, all the magic will end. You must leave before the last chime!" At the palace, shoji lanterns glowed softly, and gentle koto music floated through the grand ballroom. When Cinderella entered, everyone gasped at her grace and beauty. The Prince himself bowed politely and asked her to dance. They danced together, flowing gracefully across the polished wooden floor, and the Prince fell in love with her kind and gentle heart. They laughed and admired the feast of sekihan, mochi, and elegant wagashi sweets. But suddenly — dong, dong, dong — the great bell began to toll midnight! "Hayaku! I must go!" Cinderella cried, and she ran down the lantern-lit steps as fast as she could. One glass slipper slipped off her foot, but she had no time to stop. Behind her, the palanquin turned back into a simple kago, and the horses became little mice again. All that remained on the palace steps was one sparkling glass slipper, glinting under the moonlit sky.
story_parts.conclusion: The Prince picked up the delicate glass slipper and held it carefully in his hands. "I will find her," he promised. "This slipper will fit only her." So the Prince traveled along the lantern-lit roads to every home in the town, and all the neighbors came out to watch. When he arrived at Cinderella's wooden house, the Stepmother pushed her daughters forward. The eldest Stepsisters squeezed and squeezed their feet, but the slipper would not fit, no matter how hard they tried. "Please," said the Prince politely, "is there anyone else in this house?" The Stepmother frowned, but the Prince had already seen a quiet girl in plain clothes watching from beside the irori hearth. "Come, young lady," he said kindly. Cinderella sat down, and — slide, click — the glass slipper fit her foot perfectly, as if it had been made just for her. The Prince's face lit up with joy. "It is you! The one I danced with!" Just then, the Fairy Godmother appeared in a swirl of starlight and waved her wand once more, dressing Cinderella in her shimmering kimono gown. The Stepmother and Stepsisters bowed their heads, ashamed of how unkind they had been. But Cinderella smiled warmly at them. "Please do not worry," she said gently. "I forgive you. Let us all be happy together." The Prince and Cinderella were married at the grand castle, and there was a wonderful feast with sekihan and sweet wagashi for the whole town. Lanterns glowed, koto music played, and the koi swam happily in the pond below. And Cinderella, whose kindness and loving heart had never faded, lived happily ever after with the Prince.
